answers.fus01: Challenge 1 (Representation) has three sub-challenges: Fusion, Coordination, and Fission. Fusion combines multiple modalities into fewer (a single) representation, so #modalities > #representations. Coordination keeps one representation per modality, processed independently but coordinated, so #modalities = #representations. Fission produces more representations than input modalities, so #modalities < #representations.
answers.fus02: Additive fusion combines the modalities by a (weighted) sum: z = w1·xA + w2·xB (or fA + fB with unimodal encoders), which behaves like an ensemble / late fusion and a 1-layer network can be viewed as additive. Multiplicative fusion combines them by a product: simple multiplicative z = w·(xA × xB) or bilinear Z = W(xA^T ⊗ xB), which captures interactions/correlations between the two modalities rather than just their independent contributions.
answers.fus03: Tensor fusion forms the fused representation as the outer product of the unimodal vectors, each augmented with a constant 1, so the result captures unimodal (additive) and bimodal/higher-order (multiplicative) interactions at once. The bimodal fused tensor is Z = w·([xA;1] ⊗ [xB;1]), the outer product of the two augmented vectors. Its drawback is that the resulting weight tensor/matrix becomes very large.
answers.fus04: Low-rank Multimodal Fusion (LMF) solves the exploding size and parameter cost of plain tensor fusion (whose weight tensor grows very large). It decomposes the fusion weight tensor into low-rank, modality-specific factors, computing the fusion efficiently without ever forming the full outer-product tensor.
answers.fus05: Gated fusion weights each modality's contribution by a learned gate that depends on the inputs, e.g. z = gA(xA,xB)·xA + gB(xA,xB)·xB. The gating functions gA and gB can be seen as attention functions (data-dependent soft weights deciding how much of each modality passes through); a gate can even output a single weight for the whole modality.
answers.fus06: Early fusion first concatenates the modalities into one joint representation and then makes a single prediction. Late fusion instead makes a separate prediction per modality and combines those individual predictions/decisions at the end.
answers.fus07: Raw-modality fusion combines the modalities in their native formats (each through its own encoder, then cross-modal attention), preserving modality-specific features; it is preferred for heterogeneous data formats, when preserving features matters (e.g. medical imaging, genomics), for missing/incomplete data, for interpretability, and when compute is limited. Homogeneous fusion first transforms every modality into a common format / shared latent space and then fuses; it is preferred when a unified representation matters more than modality-specific detail, when modalities have similar structure, with pretrained embeddings, with complete data, and when there is sufficient compute.
answers.fus08: FuseMix keeps the pretrained unimodal encoders frozen and trains only lightweight fusion adapters (~1–2M parameters) to align the latent spaces, using contrastive learning plus multimodal mixup (synthetic augmentation that reduces data needs). Because there is no backprop through the large encoders, it reaches competitive performance with orders-of-magnitude less compute and data — about 600× fewer GPU days, ~80× fewer training pairs, on a single GPU.
answers.ali01: CLIP uses the InfoNCE contrastive loss. The positive pairs are matching image–text pairs (sim(z_A^i, z_B^i)); the negative pairs are the non-matching cross combinations in the batch (sim(z_A^i, z_B^j) for j≠i). The similarity is cosine similarity, and the loss pulls matched pairs together while pushing mismatched ones apart.
answers.ali02: Language grounding is tying language (words, phrases) to non-linguistic elements such as the visual world (objects, people) — e.g. associating the phrase “a woman” and “newspaper” with the corresponding regions of an image.
answers.ali03: The assignment problem assumes the same number of elements in A and B, a one-to-one “hard” alignment, and a perfect matching (every element assigned); it maximizes total similarity and can be solved exactly with linear programming / the simplex algorithm. Optimal transport relaxes these assumptions: it allows different numbers of elements and many-to-many “soft” alignment, “transporting” mass between the modalities, with the Wasserstein distance giving the optimal-transport solution.
answers.ali04: A Dynamic Time Warping path must satisfy: monotonicity (no going back in time), continuity (no gaps), boundary conditions (start and end at the matching endpoints), a warping window (stay close to the diagonal), and a slope constraint (do not insert or skip too much). It is found by dynamic programming subject to these restrictions.
answers.ali05: Hard attention selects a single discrete location/region (one glimpse); it typically needs sampling to train and is useful when compute is limited. Soft attention takes a weighted average over all locations (a distribution over locations); it is fully differentiable end-to-end and is the default in seq2seq models and transformers.
answers.ali06: CTC starts from the network's per-frame predictions, which include a special blank token (∅). The collapse rule then (1) merges consecutive duplicate labels and (2) removes the blank tokens, yielding the final label sequence (e.g. ∅ t t ah ∅ m aa aa t ow ∅ → t ah m aa t ow). CTC sums over all frame-level paths that collapse to the same label sequence, and the blank absorbs duration differences, so no pre-segmented boundaries are needed.
answers.ali07: Challenge 2 (Alignment) has three sub-challenges: Discrete Alignment (discrete elements and connections), Continuous Alignment (segmentation and continuous warping), and Contextualized Representation (alignment combined with representation).
answers.ali08: SigLIP 2 keeps global image–text coordination as its backbone but adds auxiliary objectives — captioning-based pretraining, self-distillation + masked prediction, and online data curation. Versus classic CLIP it outperforms earlier models on zero-shot classification, image–text retrieval and transfer, improves localization and dense prediction (not just global matching), and supports multiple resolutions while preserving native aspect ratio.
answers.trf01: Self-attention mixes information across tokens but is order-agnostic — by default it does not encode token position, so reordered inputs (e.g. “dog bites man” vs “man bites dog”) look like the same set of tokens just permuted. Position embeddings inject order information into the input so the model can tell different orderings apart.
answers.trf02: BERT's input representation is the sum of three embeddings per token: the token embedding, the position embedding, and the segment embedding.
answers.trf03: Masked language modeling randomly masks some input tokens ([MASK]) and trains the model to predict the original tokens using both the left and right context (bidirectional context). The loss is computed only on the masked positions.
answers.trf04: Next Sentence Prediction takes two sentences A and B (formatted [CLS] A [SEP] B [SEP]) and predicts whether B actually follows A — a binary IsNext vs NotNext classification, read from the [CLS] token's representation.
answers.trf05: The three design patterns for multimodal transformers are: One-stream (concatenate all modalities into a single shared transformer), Cross-modal (separate per-modality streams that exchange information via cross-attention), and Modality-shift (secondary modalities adjust/shift the primary modality).
answers.trf06: One-stream models like VisualBERT and UNITER concatenate the text tokens and image regions into a single joint sequence ([CLS] text tokens [SEP] region1 region2 region3) and feed it to one shared transformer encoder that applies full self-attention across both text and image tokens, producing joint text–image representations (UNITER adds richer objectives).
answers.trf07: Both use separate streams with cross-modal attention. ViLBERT has a language stream and a vision stream that exchange information through co-attention layers. LXMERT first runs unimodal encoders (a language encoder and an object encoder) and then a cross-modality encoder on top.
answers.trf08: In Vision→Language cross-modal attention, the language tokens produce the queries (Q) and the visual regions produce the keys (K) and values (V); attention = softmax(QK^T/√d). The query comes from the modality being updated (here language, which becomes visually contextualized).
answers.trf09: Masked self-attention lets each decoder position attend only to previous target tokens (future tokens are masked out), operating within the decoder's own sequence. Encoder–decoder cross-attention instead has the decoder's queries attend to all encoder outputs (decoder Q with encoder K and V), making the decoder state source-aware. A transformer decoder uses both.
answers.gen01: The three types of multimodal generation are Summarization (a reduction of information), Translation (maintenance — equal information), and Creation (an expansion of information).
answers.gen02: The multimodal generation challenge is defined as learning a generative process that produces raw modalities reflecting cross-modal interactions, structure, and coherence.
answers.gen03: DALL-E's text-to-image pipeline has two main components: (1) a discrete VAE (dVAE) that encodes images into discrete image tokens and decodes them back to images, and (2) an autoregressive transformer that, from the text tokens, generates the sequence of image tokens, which the dVAE decoder then turns into the final image.
answers.gen04: DALL-E 2 splits generation into two parts: (A) Content — coordination via CLIP, using CLIP to capture the cross-modal correspondence between text and image (producing a CLIP image embedding conditioned on the text); and (B) Generation — fully generative diffusion models that decode that CLIP embedding into the final image. So CLIP supplies the text-conditioned content/embedding and diffusion models do the image synthesis.
answers.gen05: Autoregressive models factorize the joint probability as a product of conditionals, each element conditioned on all previous ones: for an image, p(x) = ∏_i p(x_i | x_1,…,x_{i-1}) (pixel by pixel); for a sequence, p(x) = ∏_t p(x_t | x_1,…,x_{t-1}) (token by token).
answers.gen06: Creation (sub-challenge 4c) is simultaneously generating multiple modalities to increase the information content while maintaining coherence within and across modalities (requiring cross-modal interactions and temporal/causal/logical structure); it is an open challenge.
answers.gen07: Flamingo scales up the Frozen approach with much bigger models (up to ~80B-parameter language models), adds cross-attention to feed in visual features, and uses richer training data, producing a visual language model for few-shot learning.
answers.gen08: Prefix tuning conditions a frozen, pretrained language model by training only a small adapter that maps the image into embeddings used as a prefix (the conditioning signal c), so the model is steered to produce p(x|c) while the language model's weights stay frozen. Only the adapter is trained, which enables tasks like zero-shot VQA (e.g. “What color is the car?” → “Blue”).
